authoredPrompt: This figure tracks a dataset's representation through a vision transformer as a vertical stack of five flat square planes in isometric perspective, with an architecture legend up the left side. The legend alternates upward-pointing arrows with four rounded boxes, each reading ViT block x3, so consecutive planes are separated by three transformer blocks. Every plane carries the same set of plotted points, each colored by its semantic class in roughly ten hues including teal, blue, olive, green, orange, red, brown, purple, and pink. Dashed curves in matching colors connect each point to its counterpart on the plane above, so one image can be followed through the whole stack. On the bottom plane the colors are thoroughly mixed within a narrow band; the middle planes remain largely intermingled; and by the top plane the points have spread out into separate compact clumps, each a single color. Position encodes the projected embedding and color encodes class, so what the reader compares plane to plane is how tangled the colors are. The coordinates come from a t-SNE projection computed jointly across the layers shown, giving a rough view of how depth disentangles the classes.
authoredInteractions:
- Slider for network depth; the learner moves from the bottom embedding plane to the top plane, the colored point clouds update layer by layer, and it becomes clear how ViT blocks gradually untangle semantic classes.
- Hover over a class color; the learner hovers a colored cluster, matching points and dashed paths brighten across every plane, and the relationship between one semantic class and its representation trajectory becomes clear.
- Button/state for stepping through ViT block groups; the learner advances one ViT block x3 stage at a time, the corresponding plane and incoming paths highlight, and it becomes clear that separation accumulates across repeated transformer blocks.
authoredContext:
What if our data and activations are high-dimensional? The plots above only can visualize 1D and 2D data distributions. Deep representations are typically much higher-dimensional than this, and to visualize them, we need to apply tools from dimensionality reduction. These tools project the high-dimensional data to a lower dimensionality, for example 2D, which can be visualized. A common objective is to perform the projection such that the distance between two datapoints in the 2D projection is roughly proportional to their actual distance in the high-dimensional space. In the next plot, the figure, we use a dimensionality reduction technique called t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding. t-SNE ~\cite{tsne} to visualize how different layers of a modern deep net represent a dataset of images of different semantic classes, where each color represents a different semantic class. The network we are visualizing is of the transformer architecture, and we will learn about all its details in the section. For now, the important things to note are that (1) we are only showing a selected few of the layers (this net actually has dozen of layers) and (2) the embeddings are high-dimensional (in particular, they are 38,400-dimensional) but mapped down to 2D by t-SNE. Therefore, this visualization is just a rough view of what is going on in the net, unlike the visualizations in the previous section, which showed the exact embeddings and every single step of the layer-to-layer transformations.

How a powerful deep net remaps input images into a disentangled representation where semantic classes (shown in different colors) are separated. This deep net is a vision transformer (ViT~\cite{dosovitskiy2020vit}), which we will learn about in \sect{\ref{sec:transformers:ViT_arch}}. It was trained using contrastive language-image pre-training (CLIP~\cite{radford2021learning}, see \sect{\ref{sec:VLMs:CLIP}}). Each `ViT block` contains multiple layers of neural processing (see \fig{\ref{fig-transformers-ViT_arch}}; we visualize the embeddings right after the first `token norm` in a block). We apply t-SNE jointly across all shown layers.

discrepancies: Left-side ViT block boxes are much smaller and narrower than in the source, with the label text visually cramped against or spilling over the rounded outlines.
The generated stack is horizontally compressed and shifted: planes and point clouds occupy a much smaller portion of the canvas than the large right-side stack in the source.
The bottom plane has an orange active highlight that is not present in the source figure, where all plane borders are black.
The multicolored dashed trajectories and point clouds are noticeably less dense and less visually dominant than in the source, reducing the impression of many token/image trajectories through depth.
The left arrow/box architecture is not as continuous and cleanly aligned as the source's vertical arrow spine passing through the repeated ViT block labels.
evaluation.notes: The core five-plane ViT-depth representation with colored trajectories is recognizable and conceptually strong, but proportions, label sizing, and the extra orange highlight reduce visual fidelity.
action_items: Enlarge the left rounded boxes and center the 'ViT block x3' labels comfortably inside them to better match the source.
Scale up the plane stack and point/path field relative to the canvas so the right-side 3D structure dominates as in the reference.
Remove or greatly mute the orange active-plane border in the default view unless explicitly interacting with the depth slider.
Increase the density, opacity, and vertical continuity of the dashed colored trajectories to better match the source's dense flow.

feedback.rationale: The concept and interactivity are strong, but the remaining issues are implementation-level visual fixes—scale, label sizing, default highlight removal, and trajectory density—best handled by the generator.
